input: Do AI labelers grade decisions or outcomes? rlhf and rlaif
verdict: Passed the five original checks, but only one of six problems bears on the question, one generic limit slipped through, and one problem was titled with the person's own question while its quote said something else. Fixed afterwards: titles must share a meaningful word with their quotes, each key term gets its own search, results merge by relevance, and grouping drops scale-and-compute limits. Not yet run again.
search: Searching arXiv for “reward model”, “AI feedback”, “preference data”

terms.meaning: Training an AI system using rewards derived from human judgments of its outputs, typically by comparing responses and learning which ones humans prefer.
A variant of RLHF where the reward signal is generated by another AI model (often a pretrained LLM) instead of human annotators, enabling scalable feedback without direct human labeling.
Providing feedback on intermediate reasoning steps or decision-making processes rather than just final outcomes, to improve alignment and correctness in complex tasks.
Training AI systems based solely on the quality or correctness of final results, without evaluating how those results were arrived at.
The task of learning a function that predicts human preferences over AI outputs, used as a proxy reward signal in RLHF and RLAIF pipelines.

problems.title: Generalizing findings to larger model scales
statements: Owing to computational constraints, we did not scale to larger models.
Second, we only train student models in the 7-8B parameter range, so the mechanism we found may not fully explain sycophancy in larger models.
problems.explanation: The researchers could not test their findings on larger models because of limited computing power. They only experimented with models around 7-8 billion parameters, so they do not know whether the same sycophancy mechanism — where models flatter or agree with users excessively — appears in bigger models. This matters because modern AI systems are much larger, and alignment methods must work at those scales.
problems.first_step: Replicate the sycophancy investigation on a 1-2B parameter model that fits on one GPU, following the paper's experimental setup, to understand the mechanism before attempting larger scales.

problems.title: Reward models not supervising physical consistency
statements: ACWM-RM is trained to assess VQ and AF, but does not explicitly supervise physical consistency (PC).
Although RL fine-tuning with ACWM-RM maintains PC scores close to those of the pre-RL model, the reward does not directly target physical violations such as interpenetration.
problems.explanation: The reward model (ACWM-RM) was trained to judge video quality and adherence to physics, but not explicitly to check physical consistency — meaning whether objects interpenetrate or violate physical laws. Reinforcement learning with this reward kept physical consistency scores similar to before, but the reward does not directly penalize physical violations like objects passing through each other. This matters because generated videos may look plausible while containing subtle physics errors.
problems.first_step: Train a small reward model to detect physical violations (e.g., interpenetration) in generated videos, then run RL fine-tuning with this added reward signal and measure changes in physical consistency.

problems.title: Need for gradient access and vocabulary alignment in black-box reward settings
statements: Computing directional credit requires access to RM input gradients and aligned vocabularies between the actor and RM.

Future work could explore token- or sequence-alignment mechanisms across tokenizers, as well as gradient estimation for evaluators that provide only scores, to broaden the applicability of directional credit
problems.explanation: The directional credit method needs access to the reward model's input gradients and for the actor and reward model to share the same vocabulary (tokenizer). Many real-world reward models are black-box — they only return scores, not gradients — and use different tokenizers. This matters because it limits where the technique can be applied unless we can estimate gradients or align vocabularies across tokenizers.
problems.first_step: Implement a token-alignment mapping between two different tokenizers (e.g., using embedding similarity) and test gradient estimation on a small white-box model, simulating black-box conditions by hiding gradients during evaluation.

problems.title: Fine-tuned judges inheriting biases from base models on distribution-shifted outputs
statements: One unresolved hypothesis is that, on shifted policy outputs, fine-tuned judges increasingly share the preferences of their original models.
The retained Elo trajectories do not test this mechanism.
problems.explanation: When a judge model is fine-tuned to evaluate outputs, it may still carry biases from its original base model. On outputs that differ from the training distribution (distribution-shifted), these fine-tuned judges might increasingly prefer what their base model would prefer. The current Elo rating trajectories do not test this mechanism. This matters because biased judges cannot reliably evaluate new or changed model behaviors.
problems.first_step: Fine-tune a small judge model, generate outputs from a deliberately shifted policy (e.g., different topic or style), and compare the judge's preferences to the base model's preferences to quantify bias inheritance.

problems.title: AI labelers grading decisions vs outcomes in RLHF/RLAIF
statements: Our theoretical results are agnostic to model scale, so we expect the underlying mechanism to hold at larger scales as well.
problems.explanation: The authors' theoretical results do not depend on model scale, so they expect the underlying mechanism to hold at larger scales as well. However, this expectation has not been empirically verified on large models. This matters because theoretical guarantees do not always match practical behavior when models are scaled up.
problems.first_step: Implement the theoretical mechanism on a 1-2B parameter model and verify that empirical results match the theory, establishing a baseline for future large-scale validation.

problems.title: Constructing reliable ties and selecting budget k in preference learning
statements: It does not address how to construct reliable ties or how to choose the budget kk, although both decisions affect practical performance.
problems.explanation: The method does not explain how to construct reliable ties — cases where two outputs are judged equally good — or how to choose the budget k, a parameter controlling comparison effort. Both choices affect practical performance. This matters because practitioners lack guidance on these decisions, which can lead to suboptimal results.
problems.first_step: Run preference learning experiments on a small model, systematically varying tie-construction methods (e.g., random vs. similarity-based) and budget k values, then measure the impact on final model quality.
